questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was important for me to choose a destination where there were opportunities for both city-life and nature experiences. Edinburgh attracted me due to its architecture and vibe - I had been told that the scots were very friendly and open, which was also important.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had such a great experience with my exchange. Edinburgh is a good city for exchange, id say: Its easy to get to know the way around, there are good places to eat, great pubs (!), study cafés, people are welcoming and nice etc. The culture is also not very different from the danish (I guess this could be both good and bad, depending on what sort of experience you are looking for).

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Somewhat easy. I think there are help to get from the university, and there is information on their homepage. You get assigned a exchange counselour automatically and you have to have a meeting through zoom with them within the first days upon arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not recieve assistance, I think it was quite easy to figure stuff out. The structure is a lot like KU.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Although I did not get any assistance, I got the feeling that there was help to find if you needed it.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Well. Finding a place to stay was by far the worst part of exchange, I have a lot to say about it to be frank. (Officially) Edinburgh University has several uni accomodation sites. As a single semester student you are however not guarenteed accomdation through the university - but you can apply. Me and several danish students all managed to get uni accomodation - but the process was very difficult. You have to call the accomodation service directly again and again (and again). You cannot take no for an answer. It is very likely that you will first get allocated a room only a week before arriving - And it will be expensive.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I lived in a shared flat with 4 other students which I got through the university. We had our own kitchen and two bathrooms. It was not a nice place, very small bed and room - But absolutely fine for the short period that exchange is. I rarely cooked and was not home a lot.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Edinburgh is facing a housing crisis at the moment, and several students (both locals and exchange students) are not able to get accomodation, neither through the university or privately. 
I would recommend future students to accept that it will be a difficult project to find a place to stay and that you have to put in a great effort - you also really have to manage your expectations, you will probably not live somewere nice.
For private accomodation you have to be able to meet the people/see the flat in person on a very short notice - Maybe you can find a place, while staying in Edinburgh in an airbnb(hostel and visit flats.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very not satisfied. I think it is insane that it is so dificult to find somewhere to stay. I almost thought I would not be able to go because I could not find a room. I find it sad that you can go through all of the steps involved with getting accepted for exchange, and still ending up not going. I think it is so so so problematic that the responsibility falls on the individual student to relentelessly call the accomodation service. If you are a less persistant (and annoying) person than myself, you could very well end up not going.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The registration website is fine. However, the university did overbook a course and I sort of had to beg them to re-register me. I think again the key is to keep calling and calling if something with courses is not working out.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: They have a webpage were you choose which courses you want and you recieve information when it is time to fill out forms etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Again - There are phonenumbers to call, which I would recommend if you are having issues.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I ended up with the classes I wanted that KU had accepted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Calling up the university course registration team. I think that it is very possible to get the courses you want but you have to be persistant.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The experience was mixed. I had one amazing course (Ethical Values and Challenges in Care), which was so interesting, immersive and relevant. I had two courses in cognitive science to replace Cognitive Psychology at KU, which I did not enjoy as much. It is important to say that I also have very little interest in cognitive psychology. It is mandatory that I took cognitive psychology - so it is not neccesarily the fault of UoE that I was not so pleased with the courses. Cognitive science at UoE is very different from cognitive psychology at KU is my feeling from talking with people back home taking the Cognitive Psychology course.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Very mixed - the level in the cognitive psycology courses was fairly difficult, but in a different way from KU. Much more sciency/mathematical and not at all critical or social sciency as I am used to.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Similiarly to KU there are both lectures and smaller classes for discussion. I did find that the discussion classes was still more like a lecture than at KU. There are not as much of a culture for being critical about texts or theories - Its more about learning by heart.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Ethical Values and Challenges in Care
Introduction to Cognitive Science
Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience - Childhood

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Ethical Values and Challenges in Care was very interesting. It is centered around the ethics and issues you are faced with as as a professional working with people who need care. I took the course as an elective and the class consisted of nurses and students in various fields in social sciences. There was a lot of discussion and examples from real life. The person running the course, Sally Brown, was incredible at teaching. 

Developmental Cogntive Neuroscience was also interesting, it was centered on both normal and atypical cognition and brain development in children. A bit too sciency and biological for my taste. I did however include some classes regarding how aspects such as low socioeconomic status, abuse and neglect affects children, both cognitively, socially and behavioraly, which was really interesting and more relevant the interests I have in psychology. 

Introduction to Cogntive Science I would not recommend - the level and content was very mixed. Quite suprisingly a part of the course was about programming/Python, which was difficult and the connecting to psychology was hard to see. A part of the course was an introduction to philosophy of science, which seemed very introductory and unnecessary.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: If you want to join societies in cost extra. would not say that there was any expenses that I was suprised with - Maybe that the room was so expensive. I also know many other exchange student paying loads more than me, some up to 9000DKK a month.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and drinks was a bit less expensive than in Copenhagen - However, the inflation is of course also present in UK and prices were higher than usual.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is loads of societies to join at UoE: various sport societies, wine society, film society, choir etc. There is a fair in the beginning of the week were you can hear about the different activities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I joined the hillwalking society which I would recommend! They have weekend trips every other weekend to various places around Scotland.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
It is fairly easy to go to nice nature areas. There are busses going to the Pentlands, which have good easy hikes. It takes less than an hour to get there. Google 'hikes/daytrips' around edinburgh, there are plenty. There is many beautifull gardens/nature reserves to visit - look at the National Trust of Scotlands sites.
Glasgow is also only a one hour train drive away, and is also a nice city.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Fairly easy. British/scottish culture is not that different from danish. Many people living in Edinburgh are also foreigners.
I however have mostly spend time with a group of other danes also on exchange.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Good question. In some aspects I wish I had tried harder to get local friends, but it just did not happen for me. 
I think societies is a very good way to talk to different people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It found it a little difficult that people at uni are way younger than me. I am already a bit older than students at KU on the bachelor, but at UoE they are even younger. Therefore it did not make so much sense for me trying to become friends with people in my classes, since most of them are 5-7 years younger than me.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
People are very friendly and warm. I really like the pub culture, it is so cozy going to a pub and having a pint:) 
I love the aesthetic of edinburgh, very old school hoghwarts-ish. I think it is very easy to feel at home there. I could see myself living there again.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Edinburgh is an amazing city for exchange, the vibe and feeling is so cozy and nice. There are a lot of strenuous admin stuff before going (getting courses registered, finding a place to stay etc) but once you are there it is worth it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Start looking for a place to stay early, there is a lot of FB groups to join. If you are able to, maybe go for a weekend a month or so before to visit flats.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It was nice to experience living somewhere else for a long enough time for it to feel like your home. I found a good community with other danish exchange students, who were all lovely.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It can be difficult to have to be social a lot with people you dont know. I found it challenging to find a good balance between taking the alone time I needed while also pushing myself to get the most out of the experience. I think this has a lot to do with what type of person you are - Im fairly introverted, and having this temperament can be challenging during exchange. But a good learning experience also! And I would recommend fellow introverts to go on exchange aswell.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I really recommend going to Edinburgh.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
